citations.citation: "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal, 19 January 2018.
what_it_does_not_supply: NO SITE THAT AGREES WITH ITSELF, and this is why the identification stays inferred. The page's own opening line says "The Eliza Chappell School was roughly at Lake and Clark Streets are today" — which is where the school MOVED in 1834, not the log house it started in.

No way past the three-way conflict it sits in: Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake (data/structures/chappel_infant_school.json), drloih_beaubien puts the first room in Beaubien's cabin at Lake and Market, and this page carries the third reading.
No footnote, no dimension, and no description of the room itself.
what_it_supplies: THE SCHOOL'S FIRST ROOM AND THE DATE IT LEFT IT: "Chappell arrived in Chicago in June 1833 with the prospects of opening a school by September. The school was established in a small log house formerly used as a store... In 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church in Fort Dearborn, on the southwest corner of Lake and Clark Streets."
A LOG HOUSE FORMERLY USED AS A STORE is the phrase that joins to drloih_beaubien's cabin, let first to Philo Carpenter for a drug store and then, in 1833, to Chappel's school.

The school as it was kept: 25 students who furnished their own chairs, no desks, some paddling canoes across the river to it, and "maps, a globe, scriptural texts and hymn books, and illustrations of geometry and astronomy" for teaching tools.
The marriage: Chappel married the Rev. Jeremiah Porter on 15 June 1835, sixteen days before the scene date.

THE CHAPPEL SHORE DRAWING'S IMMEDIATE SOURCE (T-0909): the post's first image is the uncredited drawing deposited as eliza_chappel_school_shore_view, same filename, captioned "The Eliza Chappell School was roughly at Lake and Clark Streets are today." It republishes the drawing and supplies none of its artist, date or original publication.

citations.citation: The baptismal register of St Mary's, Chicago — the first Catholic parish in the town — opened by Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr on 22 May 1833 and read here for the years 1833, 1834 and 1835: 57 entries in French and English naming children, parents, godparents and witnesses, with the priest's own signature under every one and eight autographs of the town's own people beside them.

transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and these eleven images are photographs of it. A reading made off them is scan_verified — the higher of this project's two reading grades — and it outranks the marriage and death pages of st_cyr_register_ichr_v4, which reached this project through a 1921-22 article and a web transcription.

what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, street, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town, and names no church building on any of the eleven pages
residence, and this is the trap. A baptism documents a person at a font on a day. Presence is not residence and nothing here mints or regrades a resident
presence on 1 July 1835 for anyone not baptised or standing as sponsor within days of it
occupation. One entry writes 'Doctor Egan' — a title inside a name — and that is the only trade the book ever states

ALL CHICAGO. Entries 1-11 of 1834 were written at Bear Creek, the South Fork of the Sangamon and Springfield, in Sangamon County, on the priest's journey back from St. Louis. A reader who takes the book as a Chicago roll plants eleven households in the wrong county
reliable spelling. A French priest wrote Irish, English and German names and phoneticised Potawatomi and Odawa ones; the same woman is Nadeau, Nodeau and Nodou in his own hand on three pages
the sponsors of 1834 entry 4, which stood on a line the scan's frame cuts off
anything about 1836 or later. The two page-sides in the deposit that carry 1837-38 and 1849 entries are declared and not transcribed

The ride, its order from the forks to the fort, its reading times, its ending and the roll keepsake are modern interpretation; no visit, meeting or conversation is asserted, nobody speaks, and no interior is opened. Wolf Point and the fort are seen from public anchors.

keepsake.text: An interpretive list of the women on the ride, not a historical document.
keepsake.title: Roll of the women of 1835

opening.text: RIDE: WOMEN OF 1835. Seven stops, west to east, from the forks to the fort. Each names a woman a source puts in this town and why she still matters. Most sources of 1835 record men; these women are the ones they could not leave out. Exteriors only; nobody here speaks.

premise: Ride from Wolf Point to the fort past the places of six women a source names in the town of 1835: an author, two hotel and boarding-house keepers, a teacher and the women of two founding families.

stops.text: Wolf Point. Across the water stand the log cabins Wau-Bun puts here in 1831 as the home of Alexander Robinson and his wife's family. Catherine Chevalier Robinson was Potawatomi, granddaughter of the leader Naunongee. Her sister Archange married Antoine Ouilmette, and the village of Wilmette carries their name. Robinson descendants kept their Des Plaines land into the mid-twentieth century.

John H. Kinzie's store. His wife Juliette Kinzie later wrote Wau-Bun (1856), and its memories of 1831 are the evidence for several buildings in this very scene. On 18 June 1835, thirteen days before this date, she gave birth in Chicago to Eleanor, whose daughter Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts in 1912.

The Exchange Coffee House, Mark Beaubien's second hotel. Andreas: 'Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House.' Open under the Murphys from August 1834, it was a couple's business, and the history names Mrs. Murphy as its keeper beside her husband.

Mrs. Rufus Brown's boarding house, behind Peck's store. 'Mrs. Rufus Brown kept one of the first-class boarding houses', Andreas writes, in a town whose houses 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides.' She ran the business; the record keeps only her husband's name.

Eliza Chappel's school. She kept Chicago's first infant school, opened in 1833 in a small log house once used as a store; one account has some pupils paddling canoes across the river to class. Andreas wrote that Miss Eliza Chappel 'is entitled to especial distinction in this work.'

First Presbyterian Church. Eliza Chappel was one of its twenty-six founding members in June 1833, and on 15 June 1835 she married its pastor, Jeremiah Porter. In the Civil War, as Eliza Chappel Porter, she directed the Chicago Sanitary Commission and nursed Union wounded beside Mary Ann Bickerdyke at Chattanooga.

Fort Dearborn, from the south-west; the Beaubien homestead stands just south. Josette LaFramboise Beaubien, wife of Jean Baptiste Beaubien, was the daughter of the trader Francois LaFramboise and Shawenoqua, a Potawatomi woman. In July 1834 a Josette Beaubien stood sponsor at a baptism at St Mary's, the town's first Catholic parish.
